strengths: Well-motivated problem: Identifies genuine limitations in existing inference-time steering methods that overlook token-level causal influence
Principled methodology: Integrated Gradients choice is well-justified with clear explanation of theoretical properties (sensitivity, implementation invariance)
Comprehensive evaluation: Tests across both LLMs and VLMs, multiple safety-critical tasks, strong baselines, thorough ablations, and qualitative analysis
Consistent cross-model improvements: Demonstrates gains across diverse architectures (Llama, Qwen, LLaVA, Gemma) while preserving general capabilities
Practical efficiency: Reduces computational cost to ~96 seconds vs. 30-3600 minutes for LoRA fine-tuning
Reproducibility: Detailed experimental settings, hyperparameter analysis, GPU requirements, and full prompts in appendix
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Combines existing techniques (Integrated Gradients, PCA, activation steering) without substantial novel insight; contribution is primarily incremental
Modest improvements in many cases: FaithEval gains <1% for some models; MMHal-Bench improvements 1-5%, comparable to baselines; gains not always justify added complexity
No statistical significance testing: Single-run results without error bars or confidence intervals; unclear which improvements (ranging <1% to 13%) are statistically significant
Hyperparameter sensitivity: Non-trivial dependence on α, k, m with no principled selection method; requires development set tuning per task (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B peaks at α=6)
Limited direct validation of attribution: Relies solely on downstream task performance to validate attribution quality; no correlation with human annotations or ablations on identified tokens
Insufficient failure mode analysis: No discussion of when gradient-based attribution fails, effect of weak preference signals, or edge cases that challenge the method
Unexplored preference data sensitivity: No analysis of robustness to annotation noise or subjectivity; how does data quality affect steering?
Limited scope of steering objectives: Evaluation restricted to safety dimensions; no exploration of style, persona, factuality, or other steering goals
Weak theoretical justification: Why IG specifically? Why PCA aggregation? Method lacks formal analysis of convergence or optimality properties
Incomplete comparison with recent work: Acknowledges concurrent methods (Turner et al. 2024, Lin et al. 2025) but lacks detailed comparative analysis and differentiation
Generalization concerns: Only 2 LLM families at small-to-medium scales; unclear if findings scale to larger models or other families; multimodal applicability shown but not deeply explored
Missing code and accessibility: No mention of code release, limiting reproducibility and community adoption

strengths: Strong and consistent empirical results across both LLMs and VLMs on safety-critical benchmarks (TruthfulQA +8.44-13.22%, MMHal-Bench hallucination reduction from 0.624 to 0.514, SPA-VL preference improvements 1-5%)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple baselines, extensive ablations, hyperparameter analysis, and cross-dataset generalization studies demonstrating the robustness of design choices

Well-motivated approach addressing a genuine limitation—existing methods apply global interventions without identifying which tokens drive undesirable behaviors; the three-stage pipeline is logically coherent
Valuable multimodal extension to VLMs with modality-aware analysis (Table 13) showing how attribution differs between visual and textual tokens
Demonstrates minimal degradation of general reasoning capabilities (MMLU drop of 3.64% vs. 17.8% for CAA), addressing a key concern with steering methods
Good experimental methodology with proper hyperparameter selection, clear implementation details, and evidence of reproducibility with promised code release
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—combines well-established components (Integrated Gradients from 2017, contrastive loss, PCA, layer-wise steering) without substantial innovation in individual techniques

Computational cost of vector construction insufficiently analyzed; while Table 7 shows minimal inference-time overhead, the cost of computing steering vectors via gradient estimation and PCA is not compared against alternatives like LoRA fine-tuning

Dependence on preference data quality not thoroughly investigated; no systematic study of how attribution and steering effectiveness vary with preference data size, diversity, or quality mismatches between training and test domains

Technical justification gaps: (1) Table 8 shows vanilla gradients are nearly as effective as IG (59.75% vs 59.75%), undermining the choice of IG; (2) normalization in Eq. 5 lacks theoretical or empirical justification; (3) IG baseline selection sensitivity unexplored

Scope limitations: evaluation heavily weighted toward safety/alignment tasks; improvements on general reasoning modest (MMLU 3.64% degradation); code generation, math, and other domains not evaluated; only 3 VLM models tested

Causality vs. attribution confusion—while IG identifies influential tokens, high attribution does not guarantee that intervening on these tokens will change behavior; the paper lacks formal causal validation beyond qualitative examples

Generalization concerns: cross-dataset transfer is sometimes marginal (e.g., RealToxicity generalization); unclear how vectors generalize across model sizes, fine-tuning histories, or out-of-distribution inputs; no failure mode analysis

Baseline comparison issues: some methods show competitive performance (CAA comparable on LLM tasks), no statistical significance testing reported, and VLM baseline comparisons are limited due to fewer available methods

Design choice justification: top-k token selection varies by model (k=3 for LLMs, k=20 for VLMs) without principled explanation; layer selection for steering injection lacks intuition; modest improvements of PCA over simpler alternatives (Table 9)
